expert: Accessibility reviewer for older readers (65+, reading glasses)
first_impression: This is exactly the gift a grandchild buys a retired teacher, and the question pages are kind to tired eyes: one big question, a clear picture, plenty of white. The answer pages and the write-in parts are not. Small type, long lines, grey drawings under the smallest text and tick boxes the size of a grain of rice will lose readers over 65.

findings.issue: The smallest text on the page, the italic sources (about 7.5 pt), and the Tell someone line sit on top of grey illustration; on round-end pages so does the ROUND SCORE write-in line.
findings.why_it_matters: Low-contrast text over a grey pattern is the hardest combination for ageing eyes and for anyone with early cataracts.
findings.fix: No art behind any text: move the vignettes below the type or remove them where space is short, and print sources at no less than 8.5 pt roman.

findings.issue: Body text looks to be about 10 pt on a 70-78 character line, justified, with about 45 lines a page and close leading.
findings.why_it_matters: For readers with reading glasses, lines over about 65 characters cause lost-line errors at each return sweep, and 10 pt is at the low edge of comfortable.
findings.fix: Go to 11 pt on 14.5-15 pt leading with a 60-65 character measure (this adds pages; trimming the closing summary paragraphs recovers most of them), or publish a separate large-print edition at 14 pt and link the two on Amazon.

findings.issue: The line the reader is told to read aloud is set in italic, at body size or a little under, beside a small grey megaphone.
findings.why_it_matters: Italic is noticeably harder to read for low-vision readers, and this is the line read aloud at the table, often in dimmer light.
findings.fix: Set Tell someone in roman, semibold, 1-2 pt larger than the body, with no hyphenation.

findings.issue: The TRUE / FOLKLORE / DISPUTED boxes are tick squares of about 3 mm, and the SURE and GUESSING boxes are about 2 mm, labelled in light monospace of about 6-7 pt.
findings.why_it_matters: Older hands with a ballpoint cannot tick a 2 mm square cleanly, and the labels are below comfortable reading size.
findings.fix: Make every tick box at least 5-6 mm, set the labels at 9 pt in a medium weight, and give SURE and GUESSING the same box size as the verdict options.

findings.issue: The score table gives each round a row of ten tiny squares (about 3 mm) plus a small '/10' box in light monospace.
findings.why_it_matters: It is the page people return to most, and ten tiny boxes in a row are hard to count and fill.
findings.fix: Replace the ten squares with one large write-in box per round (at least 12 x 8 mm) and set '/10' at 10 pt.

findings.issue: Running heads, 'ROUND 1 · No. 1', 'YOUR CALL', 'ANSWER OVERLEAF', page numbers and the contents page numbers are all in a thin, widely tracked monospace at about 6.5-7.5 pt, and the page numbers sit beside a grey icon.
findings.why_it_matters: These labels are how readers find their way around the book; thin small mono loses contrast first as eyesight ages.
findings.fix: Raise all labels to 8.5 pt minimum in a regular or medium weight (not light), and set page numbers in the text face at 9 pt without the grey icon beside them.

findings.issue: The instruction says 'Write each team's name on the line, its score in the box', but there is no name line; the lines on the page belong to rounds R1-R10.
findings.why_it_matters: Instructions that do not match the form cause hesitation, especially for less confident players.
findings.fix: Add a clear write-in line under 'Team A' and 'Team B' labelled 'Team name', or change the instruction to match the page.

keep: The question pages: large serif question, one picture and plenty of white space.
The gift page on p.3 with generous lines to write on.
Black text on white for the body, with no colour-dependent meaning anywhere in the interior.
The tick and cross symbols for TRUE and FOLKLORE, which are clear at any size.
sign_off_reason: Clear the art from under text and enlarge the tick boxes before print; plan a large-print edition for the gift market.
